title: Suspected Spinal Cord Compression: Red Flags and Urgent Imaging

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with cancer and suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC): red flags, contact with the MSCC coordinator, whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 hours, dexamethasone, analgesia, immobilisation and definitive treatment. findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.

unverifiedSections: NICE NG234 gives dexamethasone 16 mg only for haematological malignancy with spinal metastases; the 16 mg daily MSCC dose comes from the West Midlands palliative care page, which names no gastric protection drug or dose.
NICE NG234 gives no analgesic doses and no thromboprophylaxis advice in the extracts opened.

pathophysiology.summary: Spinal metastases or an epidural mass compress the spinal cord or cauda equina, causing progressive loss of neurological function. Severe, progressive, night or mechanical spinal pain in a person with cancer should prompt advice from the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours. Neurological symptoms with a history of cancer are an oncological emergency requiring immediate contact with the MSCC coordinator. Spinal stability determines whether the person can sit up or weight bear.

clinicalManagement.title: Contact the MSCC coordinator
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately for neurological signs; within 24 hours for pain only
actions: Treat neurological symptoms with cancer as an oncological emergency.
Consider spinal immobilisation for moderate to severe movement-related pain; nurse supine.

clinicalManagement.title: Whole-spine MRI
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible and within 24 hours
actions: Image the whole spine; overnight MRI only when needed to start treatment immediately.

clinicalManagement.title: Corticosteroid
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible after assessment
actions: West Midlands: dexamethasone 16 mg orally daily while treatment is planned; NICE gives 16 mg orally (or equivalent) for haematological malignancy.
Stop dexamethasone if given before imaging and MSCC is ruled out.

clinicalManagement.title: Definitive treatment
actions: Radiotherapy as soon as possible and within 24 hours if not suitable for surgery; 8 Gy single fraction unless high risk.
Offer surgery as soon as possible to halt neurological decline when appropriate.

clinicalManagement.title: Stability and mobilisation
actions: Seek expert advice within 24 hours and start a stability assessment.
If stable, graded sitting then weight bearing; monitor symptoms.

regimens.indication: Suspected or confirmed metastatic spinal cord compression with neurological signs
regimens.frequency: Daily (loading 16 mg as soon as possible after assessment)
regimens.duration: Continue while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy; then reduce gradually over 5–7 days and stop
adjustments: Increase dose temporarily if neurological function deteriorates.
NICE: do not routinely give without neurological signs except as part of a radiotherapy regimen; consider for severe pain or haematological malignancy.
Equivalent parenteral dose can be used (NICE).
monitoring: Blood glucose in all patients on corticosteroids.
Neurological status; gastric protection should be considered.
contraindications: Stop if MSCC and spinal metastases are ruled out.
Cautions such as diabetes and peptic ulcer are in the corticosteroid chapter; not detailed in the source opened.
